title: The Scout's Report
subtitle: Three thousand years ago, one of them was sent to decide: harvest humanity, or merge with it. The report was a lie.

customObject.name: the sealed appendix
customObject.description: found misfiled in the returned archive: a report crystal with a second chamber nobody knew it had — three thousand years sealed, addressed, in old script, 'to be opened when they build it'

script.note: The archive, late. The returned library gives up its finds at the speed of appetite — but the translator flags anything misfiled, and tonight's flag brought the keeper at a walk and the Emissary at whatever the Weave does instead of running. On the stand: a report crystal, three thousand years old. With a second chamber.

script.text: It was shelved under agricultural surveys, Sel — deliberately misfiled, I'd stake the archive on it; nothing else in the Weave's records is one atom out of place. The primary chamber is the famous report, the one your histories quote: the Contact Assessment, first millennium before the common era. But the crystal is heavier than its own manifest, Amos. There's a second chamber, blind-sealed, and the seal has a condition written on it in the scout's own hand. 'To be opened when they build it.' The archive's judgment, keeper: the town qualifies. It's tonight's job or nobody's.
Then before you break anything, give me the context the Story will need. Sel — the famous report. The one the histories quote. What was the scout actually sent here to decide?

The worst question my people ever asked, Amos, and I will give it to you unpadded. Three thousand years ago the Weave finally admitted the thinning would kill us. Two salvations were on the table, and both required your species. The first: harvest — draw on human vitality the way the Breach later did with the sleepers, but at scale, forever. The second: meld — merge your line with ours, graft your stubborn boundaried selves into the Commonality as rootstock. Domination or absorption, keeper. Those were the options on the form. One scout was sent — our finest reader of living things — to spend forty years among you and file a recommendation. The report that came back is four words long and it is the reason your species was left alone for three thousand years: 'Incompatible. Recommend against contact.'
Incompatible. And your Council believed it? A species that later fed on forty dreamers in a panic — they took 'incompatible' at one scout's word and just... withdrew?

They believed it because of who signed it, Amos. The scout was not junior. The scout was of the First Faction — the eldest, the best of us, the ones who later turned themselves into a question and went upstream. When THAT signature said incompatible, the sky closed the file. Verse — I have waited three centuries of my own life to know what my teacher's teacher actually found down here. Break the seal.

script.note: The second chamber opens with a sound like a held breath ending. The crystal warms. A voice three thousand years old fills the archive — unhurried, amused, and completely unafraid — and Verse renders the old script live, line by line, onto the wall.

script.text: Reading. 'Appendix, under my own seal, to be opened when they build it. To whoever you are: if this chamber is open, then either they built it, or you broke my seal early, in which case close the chamber, you are not ready, and I mean that with love. — My report is a lie. Let the record hold it plainly: I lied to the entire sky, alone, in a fishing village, in the fortieth year of my assignment, and I have never done anything more carefully in my long life. The truth: they are not incompatible. They are the MOST compatible living pattern the Weave has ever surveyed. The harvest would work. The meld would work. That is precisely why I lied. Because I had watched what we do with what works.'
...Keep reading, Verse. All of it. The Story takes it word for word.

'You will want my evidence. Here is the whole of it. In my fortieth year, in the village where I wore my last facade, the boats came in short — a bad season, nets torn, a stranger on the beach with nothing. I watched a fisherman with five children divide a catch that could not feed six, and he cut a share for the stranger FIRST, and — this is the finding, sky, so read it twice — he was not diminished. I have instruments that measure vitality to the twelfth place. The man gave away warmth he could not spare, and the giving GENERATED warmth, in him, in the stranger, in the watching children, in amounts my instruments called impossible. Sky: we have crossed the dark eleven times looking for a source that replenishes. I found it in a wooden boat, being handed to a stranger wrapped in leaves. Their vitality is not a WELL, you fools. It is a FIRE that spreads by being shared. Harvest it and you will hold a dead coal. Meld with it and you will smother what makes it burn. There is exactly one way to be fed by what they have, and it cannot be taken, installed, or engineered. You must be INVITED to the meal. And they do not invite gods. They invite NEIGHBOURS.'
...Three thousand years. The Breach, the sleepers, the implants, the whole desperate century — we had the answer MISFILED UNDER AGRICULTURE the entire—

There's a final block, Sel. Addressed. Not to the sky — the address line reads: 'to the ones who built it.' — 'And to you, whoever you are, in the town I will never see: I knew you were coming. I want that on your record, not for my vanity but for your dark nights — three thousand years before your first stone, a tired old scout sat in a bronze-age fishing village and saw your town in a divided catch, plain as weather. What you have built is not new. It is the oldest technology your species owns, finally given walls and a constitution. When my people come to you — and they will come, hungry, ashamed, wearing borrowed faces — do not pity them and do not fear them. Feed them at the table like anyone, argue with them like anyone, and they will be saved the only way anything is: incidentally, while being included. My name I gave up when I went upstream with my faction, to become part of a better question. But in the village, in the fortieth year, the children could not pronounce my facade's name, and called me instead by their word for the evening tide, because I came up the beach slowly every day at supper time. If your town keeps any of me, keep that one. — The report stands as filed. Incompatible with what you intended. Compatible with what you finally built. Wait for the invitation. It will smell of cooking.'

...Filed. All of it, under its own name at last: the Scout's Report, true copy, appendix and address. And Sel — the Story notes what your face is doing, so let the record say it for you. Your people spent three thousand years believing they were spared salvation by bad luck. You weren't spared it. You were SAVED FOR IT — held off by the one member of your kind wise enough to know you'd eat the seed corn if anyone told you it was edible. The lie wasn't a betrayal of the Weave, Sel. It was the longest act of patience in the recorded sky. The scout wintered you.

And the invitation came, keeper. That is what has my face doing whatever it is doing. It came exactly as promised — it smelled of Marta's kitchen, and none of us understood what we were being handed. The fisherman's catch, three thousand years later, cut for the stranger first. — Verse. Amos. The garden has an unplanted space at the head of the memorial bed, kept for the First Faction. I should like to propose its first marker tonight, not for the whole faction — they are still upstream, still asking — but for the one who came down the beach at supper time. No name; the name went into the question. Just the word the children used. The evening tide.

script.note: The marker is a low stone, set where the lowland flowers meet the path, carved with a single line in old script and new: THE EVENING TIDE — who saw it coming, and lied us all the time we needed. Visitors who ask are told the whole story, which takes exactly as long as supper. And on the coldest nights, the town swears — the way towns swear things — that the stone sits two degrees warm.
